section.title: A New Heart and a New Spirit
section.sectionRationale: This is the Old Testament's clearest statement of the new covenant hope: not for Israel's sake but for His own holy name, profaned among the nations by their exile, God promises to gather His people, sprinkle clean water on them, give them a new heart and a new spirit, and put His own Spirit within them so they can finally keep His statutes from the inside out.
section.thesis: God acts to save His people not because they deserve it but to vindicate His own holy name, promising a cleansing, a new heart, and His own indwelling Spirit that will finally make obedience possible from within, a new covenant fulfilled in Christ's blood and poured out at Pentecost.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Israel's defilement of the land and God's holy name profaned among the nations; the great promise itself, gathering, cleansing, a new heart, a new spirit, and God's own Spirit given; and the land made like the garden of Eden, filled again with flocks of returning people.

units.label: Why God acts: not for your sake
units.note: the exile explained, and God's name profaned among the nations

verses.text: Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, when the people of Israel lived in their land, they defiled it by their own ways and deeds. Their behavior before Me was like the uncleanness of a woman's impurity.
So I poured out My wrath upon them because of the blood they had shed on the land, and because they had defiled it with their idols.
I dispersed them among the nations, and they were scattered throughout the lands. I judged them according to their ways and deeds.
And wherever they went among the nations, they profaned My holy name, because it was said of them, ‘These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land.’
But I had concern for My holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations to which they had gone.

units.label: A new heart, a new spirit
units.note: cleansing, transformation, and God's own indwelling Spirit

verses.text: Therefore tell the house of Israel that this is what the Lord GOD says: It is not for your sake that I will act, O house of Israel, but for My holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you went.

I will show the holiness of My great name, which has been profaned among the nations, the name you have profaned among them. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, declares the Lord GOD, when I show My holiness in you before their eyes.
For I will take you from among the nations and gather you out of all the countries, and I will bring you back into your own land.
I will also sprinkle {{mayim_tehorim|clean water}} on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols.
I will give you a {{lev_chadash|new heart}} and put a {{ruach_chadashah|new spirit}} within you; I will remove your heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.
And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances.
Then you will live in the land that I gave your forefathers; you will be My people, and I will be your God.
I will save you from all your uncleanness. I will summon the grain and make it plentiful, and I will not bring famine upon you.
I will also make the fruit of the trees and the crops of the field plentiful, so that you will no longer bear reproach among the nations on account of famine.
Then you will remember your evil ways and wicked deeds, and you will loathe yourselves for your iniquities and abominations.
It is not for your sake that I will act, declares the Lord GOD, let it be known to you. Be ashamed and disgraced for your ways, O house of Israel!

units.label: The land like the garden of Eden
units.note: cities rebuilt, flocks of people filling a resettled land

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says: On the day I cleanse you from all your iniquities, I will cause the cities to be resettled and the ruins to be rebuilt.
The desolate land will be cultivated instead of lying desolate in the sight of all who pass through.
Then they will say, ‘This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden. The cities that were once ruined, desolate, and destroyed are now fortified and inhabited.’
Then the nations around you that remain will know that I, the LORD, have rebuilt what was destroyed, and I have replanted what was desolate. I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it.
This is what the Lord GOD says: Once again I will hear the plea of the house of Israel and do for them this: I will multiply their people like a flock.
Like the numerous flocks for sacrifices at Jerusalem during her appointed feasts, so the ruined cities will be filled with flocks of people. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

mayim_tehorim.gloss: Clean water, evoking the ceremonial washings of the Levitical law applied here to the whole nation's moral defilement, anticipating the washing of regeneration in the New Testament.

lev_chadash.gloss: A new heart, replacing a heart of stone with a heart of flesh, soft and responsive to God rather than dead toward Him. Jesus points Nicodemus back to this promise when He speaks of the new birth, John 3.

ruach_chadashah.gloss: A new spirit. Paired here with God's own Spirit put within His people, this promise anticipates the New Testament gift of the Holy Spirit, who enables obedience from within rather than mere external conformity.

basic.context: Israel defiled its own land with bloodshed and idols, so God scattered them among the nations, where His holy name was profaned rather than honored: 'these are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land.' In response God makes His clearest promise yet: not for Israel's sake but for His own name's sake, He will gather them, cleanse them with water, remove their heart of stone, give them a heart of flesh and a new spirit, and put His own Spirit within them so they finally walk in His statutes.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical promise of return from Babylonian exile, but its language, a new heart, a new spirit, God's own Spirit causing obedience, clearly reaches beyond mere geographic return to a change no resettlement of land could accomplish by itself. The New Testament treats this promise as fulfilled in the new covenant secured by Christ and applied by the Holy Spirit, not merely in the physical return under Ezra and Nehemiah.
basic.originalLanguages: The promise centers on a lev chadash, new heart, and ruach chadashah, new spirit, replacing a heart of stone with a heart of flesh. This is prepared for by sprinkling mayim tehorim, clean water, on the people, cleansing them from impurities and idols. Only after this cleansing and heart transplant does God put 'My Spirit' within them, causing them to walk in His statutes, a decisive shift from external command to internal enabling.
basic.typology: The sprinkling of clean water anticipates the washing of regeneration in the New Testament, Titus 3:5, Hebrews 10:22. The new heart and new spirit are directly identified by Jesus as the new birth necessary to see the kingdom of God, and Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel, is rebuked for not recognizing this very passage, John 3:3-10.
basic.christ: Jesus explicitly builds His teaching on the new birth in John 3 on this passage: when He tells Nicodemus, 'unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,' He is pointing a teacher of Israel back to exactly this promise of cleansing water and God's own Spirit given. Paul traces his ministry's power directly to what this passage promises, a new covenant 'not in a written code but in the Spirit', 2 Corinthians 3:3-6, secured by Christ's blood, Luke 22:20, and inaugurated at Pentecost, Acts 2.
basic.god: God's motive here is startling and freeing: 'it is not for your sake that I will act... but for My holy name.' His mercy is not first a response to Israel's merit but a vindication of His own character and word before a watching world. Yet that same zeal for His name produces the most personal, intimate promise in the Old Testament, a heart transplant and an indwelling Spirit, showing that God's glory and His people's deepest good are never actually in competition.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises the same new covenant, God's law written on the heart. John 3:3-10 shows Jesus rebuking Nicodemus for missing this very passage. 2 Corinthians 3:3-6 contrasts the letter that kills with the Spirit who gives life. Titus 3:5 describes salvation as the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Spirit.
basic.oneStory: This is one of Scripture's clearest new covenant promises: God will act not for Israel's sake but for His own name, cleansing His people, giving them a new heart and His own indwelling Spirit so obedience finally flows from within. Christ secures this covenant by His blood, and the Spirit poured out at Pentecost begins its fulfillment, turning hearts of stone into hearts that love and follow God at last.

context.literary:
This passage is the second of the three great restoration panels in chapters 34 to 37, and it is the hinge between the restored land of 36:1-15 and the raised bones of chapter 37. It opens with the word-event formula in verse 16 and follows a clear argument. Verses 16 to 21 give the diagnosis and the reason for exile. Verses 22 to 32 give the promise, framed on both sides by the sentence 'It is not for your sake that I will act', in verses 22 and 32. Verses 33 to 38 describe the result, the land like Eden and the cities full of people.

The frame is the key to its meaning. The repeated denial of verses 22 and 32 sits at the beginning and end of the promise, so that every gift in between, the gathering, the cleansing, the new heart and the Spirit, is wrapped in the statement that God is not rewarding Israel. The promises themselves are arranged in a sequence that moves from outside to inside: bring them from the nations, sprinkle them with water, give a new heart, put in My Spirit, and then bring them to live in the land, verses 24 to 28. The order matters. The land comes last, after the cleansing and the inner change.

A line that is easy to miss is verse 31, where the people 'will remember your evil ways and wicked deeds, and you will loathe yourselves'. Shame comes after the promise, not before it. Many of us expect repentance to be the condition of grace, and here the gift of grace produces the shame, and the shame is the sign that the heart has been changed.

The unit closes with its own pair of images, the land like the garden of Eden, verse 35, and the people like the flocks brought to Jerusalem for the feasts, verse 38. It joins the sanctuary and the garden, and it ties back to chapter 34, where the people were already a flock.
context.historical:
The setting is the exile, and the accusation of verses 17 to 20 is a theological explanation of it. The image 'the uncleanness of a woman's impurity' in verse 17 comes from the purity laws, where a woman during her period was ceremonially unclean, Leviticus 15:19. It speaks of defilement that makes a person unfit to approach the sanctuary, and Ezekiel, who was a priest, uses it with force. The land itself was defiled by bloodshed and idols, as Numbers 35:33 says bloodshed pollutes the land, and Leviticus 18:24-28 warns that the land will vomit out those who defile it.

The charge of verse 20, that Israel 'profaned My holy name' among the nations, rests on how the ancient world read events. A nation's defeat was taken as a defeat of its god. When Judah was carried off, the surrounding peoples said, 'These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land.' The exile therefore did damage to the reputation of God, and Isaiah 52:5 and Paul's quotation of it in Romans 2:24 say that the blasphemy of the nations came from Israel's behaviour.

The promises borrow from rituals that Ezekiel's first hearers knew well. The sprinkling of water in verse 25 echoes the water of purification made with the ashes of a red heifer, Numbers 19:9 and 19:17-19, which cleansed those made unclean by contact with death. In Psalm 51:7 David prays to be purified with hyssop. The promise of a new heart answers the standing problem recorded in Deuteronomy 29:4, that the LORD 'has not given you a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear', and in Jeremiah 17:1 and 9, where sin is engraved on the heart.

The final image of verse 38, the flocks for sacrifices at the feasts in Jerusalem, recalls the crowds of animals driven into the city at Passover and the pilgrim feasts. A hearer in exile, who had not seen the temple for years, would feel the abundance of that picture.
context.canonical:
The central promise of a new heart is one of the great texts of the Old Testament, and it has many companions. Deuteronomy 30:6 says the LORD will circumcise the hearts of the people and their descendants so that they will love Him, and Jeremiah 31:33 promises that He will put His law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. Jeremiah 32:39 speaks of 'one heart and one way'. Ezekiel's own book says it three times, in 11:19-20, in 18:31 where the people are told to make themselves a new heart, and here in 36:26-27, where God says He will give it.

The Spirit's role grows through the book. Ezekiel is carried and set on his feet by the Spirit, 2:2 and 3:24, and in the next chapter the Spirit enters the dry bones, 37:14. Ezekiel 39:29 says God will pour out His Spirit on the house of Israel, and Joel 2:28 widens the promise to all people. Isaiah 44:3 joins the water and the Spirit in a single promise: 'I will pour water on the thirsty land... I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants.'

The New Testament identifies the fulfilment plainly. Jesus asks Nicodemus, 'You are Israel's teacher, and you do not understand these things?', John 3:10, after speaking of being born of water and the Spirit in 3:5. Paul writes to the Corinthians that they are 'a letter from Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts', 2 Corinthians 3:3, and that God has made him a minister of a new covenant, 3:6. Hebrews 8:10 and 10:16-17 quote Jeremiah's new covenant, and Titus 3:5 speaks of 'the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit'. At Pentecost Peter says that Joel's promise is fulfilled, Acts 2:17 and 2:33, and Galatians 3:14 calls the Spirit 'the promise'.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's message is aimed at an exile community that may have believed a more comfortable story. One version held that the exile was a mistake and that God would soon restore them for their merit, and another held that the exile showed the LORD was beaten. The prophet answers both. The exile was a just sentence for real defilement, and the return will come, but not because the people have earned it. It will come because the name of God has been dragged through the nations and He will clear it.

The heart of the message, then, is that restoration cannot be a mere repair of circumstances. If the people returned to the land with the same hearts, the story would repeat. So the promise is of a change deeper than geography. God will deal with their guilt by cleansing, and with their nature by a new heart and His own Spirit. The point of the stress on God's name is to dislodge their confidence in themselves and place it where it belongs.

He also meant the exiles to feel the weight of verses 31 and 32: shame, real self-loathing for what they had done, and the understanding that mercy is not a reward. That is a tender and demanding word. It tells hearers that they cannot repair their standing, and that for the same reason they cannot be ruled out of it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is a promise, a list of what God says He will do, and nearly every verb in verses 24 to 30 has God as its subject. It is descriptive of His intention and not a set of instructions for the reader. The right response to a promise is trust and thanks, not an attempt to produce the new heart by effort. Ezekiel 18:31 does command, 'fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit', and the two texts belong together: the command shows what is required and the promise shows who supplies it.

What does carry forward is the shape of God's work. He cleans, He changes the heart, He gives His Spirit, and the result is obedience. The New Testament teaches believers to expect this pattern and to work within it: 'work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you', Philippians 2:12-13. Obedience in the life of a believer is therefore neither the way to earn the new heart nor optional once it has been given.

The land and harvest promises of verses 28 to 38 need the same care as those in the earlier chapters. They were given to Israel about a particular place, and the New Testament treats them as pointing to a wider inheritance. A reader should neither claim every material blessing as a personal entitlement nor dismiss the physical promises as mere symbols.

debates.question: When and how is this promise fulfilled?

views.label: In the new covenant in Christ and the church
views.case: The New Testament applies the language directly: the new birth of John 3:3 to 10, the Spirit given at Pentecost, Acts 2:33, the heart tablets of 2 Corinthians 3:3 and the new covenant of Hebrews 8:10. On this view Ezekiel 36:25 to 27 is fulfilled in every believer who is cleansed and given the Spirit, whether Jew or Gentile, and the land language is carried to the world and the new creation.

views.label: Partly in the return from exile, fully in Christ
views.case: The return under Cyrus began the gathering of verse 24, but the post-exilic community did not have the deep change promised in verses 26 and 27. Ezra and Nehemiah show a people who confessed the same old sins, Nehemiah 9. This view sees the return as a first stage whose inner reality waited for the Spirit.

views.label: Initially in the church, finally in a restored Israel
views.case: Others hold that the spiritual promises are fulfilled in the church now, but that the promise of regathering and of a new heart for the nation Israel will find a further fulfilment, as Paul suggests in Romans 11:26 to 29, where he says that the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the promise is rooted in the new covenant and that Christ is the one through whom the Spirit is given. The passage itself stresses the manner of fulfilment, God's own initiative and indwelling, more than its schedule.

debates.question: Does the new heart come before faith, or after it?

views.label: God's gift of life comes first and produces faith
views.case: The verbs of 36:26 and 27 are all God's, and a heart of stone cannot respond until it is replaced. Ephesians 2:4 and 5 says God made us alive when we were dead, and John 6:44 says no one can come unless the Father draws. Many in the Reformed tradition read the sequence as regeneration preceding faith, with the two so closely joined in experience that they cannot be separated in time.

views.label: God's grace enables a free response
views.case: Others, in the Arminian tradition, hold that God's prior grace makes a response possible, but that the person freely receives or refuses it. They point to the commands to repent and believe, including Ezekiel 18:31, and to the way verse 31 here has shame following the promise.

views.label: Command and gift held together
views.case: A third approach notes that Scripture does not resolve the order in a single formula. It commands, as in Ezekiel 18:31, and it promises, as here, and Paul puts them side by side in Philippians 2:12 and 13.

debates.bearing: Whatever the logic of the order, the text puts the whole weight on God's action. The proper response is gratitude and obedience, and no reader should take comfort from the thought that the change is his own achievement.

debates.question: What is the 'water' of verse 25, and of John 3:5?

views.label: Ritual cleansing fulfilled in the Spirit's work
views.case: The sprinkling echoes the purification water of Numbers 19. Hebrews 9:13 and 14 draws the line from that water to the blood of Christ who purifies the conscience, and Titus 3:5 speaks of the washing of new birth. On this view 'water and Spirit' in John 3:5 is a single idea of inner cleansing by the Spirit.

views.label: Baptism
views.case: Many in the church's history, including the early fathers, read the water of John 3:5 as baptism, with Ezekiel 36:25 as its background. Hebrews 10:22 mentions both sprinkled hearts and bodies washed with pure water.

views.label: The word of God or physical birth
views.case: Others take 'water' as the word, as in Ephesians 5:26, or as natural birth, as in John 3:6. Ezekiel's own text is about cleansing from impurities and idols and does not mention baptism.

debates.bearing: The Ezekiel background shows that the water stands for cleansing from sin, and the Spirit for the new life that follows. Believers differ on how baptism relates to it, but all agree that what the water symbolises is the work of God.

study.originalLanguages:
The accusation of verse 17 uses the language of the purity laws, with 'uncleanness' and 'impurity' (niddah), the term for the separation of a woman during her period, Leviticus 15:19. It is not a comment on women but a picture of how defilement works, a condition that bars a person from the sanctuary until it is dealt with. In verse 20, 'they profaned My holy name' uses the verb chalal, to make common or desecrate, which Leviticus 22:32 forbids with the very same object, 'My holy name'. Israel was the carrier of the name, and its behaviour made the name common.

The promise to cleanse in verse 25 uses the verb zaraq, to sprinkle or scatter, and the cleansing is of 'all your impurities and all your idols'. The pairing is notable, since the people are cleansed of both ritual uncleanness and idolatry. The Torah's purification water in Numbers 19:17-19 is sprinkled on the unclean person, and Ezekiel's promise of 'clean water' draws on that image, with God as the one who sprinkles.

The new heart of verse 26 is the focus. The word for 'heart', lev, is not the seat of feelings alone. In Hebrew thought it is the centre of thought, will and loyalty, so a change of heart is a change of mind and desire. The contrast is between 'heart of stone' (lev ha'even) and 'heart of flesh' (lev basar), the hard and unresponsive replaced by the soft and living. In 18:31 the people are commanded to make themselves a new heart and a new spirit. In 36:26 God says 'I will give' it. The same verb 'give' (natan) stands behind the 'put' of the next verse, 'I will put My Spirit within you', so the one word of giving carries both gifts.

The word ruach, 'spirit', does a good deal of work. Here it is first a 'new spirit' within the person and then 'My Spirit', the Spirit of God. In the same book the word means wind, breath and Spirit all together, and in chapter 37 the play on the three senses is the heart of the vision of the bones. In verse 27 the person is not left alone with his new inner life. God's own Spirit is placed 'within you', in your midst, so that the gift becomes a presence.

The purpose clause in verse 27, 'cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances', shows that obedience is the result. 'Walk' is the standard verb for a way of life, and 'observe' is the verb for guarding or keeping. The language of Deuteronomy for keeping the law is now promised as something God will accomplish in His people. The same pairing of statutes and ordinances occurs in 11:20, where the new heart is also in view, with the result that 'they may follow My statutes' and 'be My people'.

The covenant formula of verse 28, 'you will be My people, and I will be your God', is the oldest summary of the relationship, and in Ezekiel it follows the gift of the heart, not the other way around. Verse 31 closes the movement with the verb to loathe, as in 6:9, where the survivors 'will loathe themselves', and with the shame of 16:63. The people's moral sense is restored by the gift.

typology.fulfillment: The water of purification in Numbers 19, made with the ashes of a heifer, cleansed those who had contacted death, and Ezekiel promises that God Himself will sprinkle Israel with clean water. The New Testament says the ritual cleansed the body, but the blood of Christ 'will purify our consciences from works of death', Hebrews 9:13-14, and it speaks of hearts sprinkled to cleanse a guilty conscience, Hebrews 10:22. Believers are 'washed' in the name of the Lord Jesus and the Spirit of God, 1 Corinthians 6:11. The type falls short in that its water dealt with ceremonial defilement and needed repeating, while the cleansing in Christ deals with the conscience and is once for all.

typology.type: The heart of stone and the heart of flesh
typology.fulfillment: The two hearts describe the human condition and its cure. Stone is the hard heart of a house that is hard-headed and hard-hearted, Ezekiel 3:7, and flesh is the heart that can respond. Paul describes the unrenewed mind as hostile to God and unable to submit, Romans 8:7-8, and says that the Spirit gives life, Romans 8:9-11. In Christ the transplant is real: 'if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation', 2 Corinthians 5:17. The type, like the law that preceded it, could show the need without supplying it, and Ezekiel's promise looks beyond itself to the one who sends the Spirit.

The promise 'I will put My Spirit within you' goes beyond the earlier experience in which the Spirit came upon chosen leaders. It anticipates what Jesus tells His disciples about the Spirit who 'abides with you and will be in you', John 14:17. At Pentecost Peter says Jesus 'has received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear', Acts 2:33, and Galatians 3:14 calls the Spirit the promise of the blessing to Abraham. Paul says the Spirit of Christ lives in believers, Romans 8:9. The Old Testament form is limited to a nation, while the fulfilment is for all who believe.

typology.type: The land like the garden of Eden
typology.fulfillment: The remark of the nations in verse 35, that the land 'has become like the garden of Eden', pictures a return to the first creation, and Isaiah 51:3 makes the same promise. It points beyond the post-exilic land to the new creation, where the tree of life stands by the river and the curse is gone, Revelation 22:1-3, and where God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. The type is restricted by place and by time, and what it signifies is a renewed earth under the rule of Christ.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most directly through the new covenant. Jesus at the Last Supper says, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you', Luke 22:20. The covenant He means is the one Jeremiah announced and Ezekiel describes, with forgiveness and a law written on the heart. The new heart and the Spirit are not separate from His work. They are purchased by it. Paul says that Christ redeemed us so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit, Galatians 3:14, and the Spirit is given because the Son has been glorified, John 7:39.

The second line is the cleansing. The sprinkling of clean water in verse 25 is answered by the death of the Lamb, since 'the blood of Christ... purify our consciences from works of death', Hebrews 9:14. Ezekiel could promise cleansing, but he could not say how a holy God could cleanse the guilty without ignoring the guilt. The cross is the answer. God is both 'just and the justifier', and the water that He sprinkles is applied through a death.

The third line is the one Jesus draws Himself. In John 3 He tells Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom of God unless born again, and that no one can enter it unless 'born of water and the Spirit', verses 3 and 5. When Nicodemus asks 'How can this be?' Jesus answers, 'You are Israel's teacher, and you do not understand these things?', verses 9 and 10. The reproach makes sense only if Israel's teachers should have known the promise of Ezekiel 36. Jesus is saying that the hope was written in their own scriptures and that He is bringing it.

The fourth line is the motive. God acts 'for My holy name', and in Christ this is seen as the glory of the Father. Jesus teaches His disciples to pray 'hallowed be Your name', Matthew 6:9, and the cross is where the holiness and the love of God are shown together. The name that the exiles profaned is honoured in a Son who obeyed.

Last, the Eden land of verse 35 leads to the one who makes all things new, Revelation 21:5. Christ is the second Adam who brings the life that the first Adam's fall lost, Romans 5:17 and 1 Corinthians 15:45, and the garden promised in Ezekiel is the garden restored through Him. One caution is due. The chapter does not describe the cross or name the Messiah. The links to Christ rest on how the New Testament itself reads Ezekiel 36, and on the way its themes find their completion in Him.
study.god:
The most surprising line in the chapter is the one God says twice: 'It is not for your sake that I will act', verses 22 and 32. It strips away every ground of boasting. The God who speaks is not an indulgent father waiting for the children to behave. He has seen the defilement, judged it, and scattered the people. Nothing in the people's record would move Him now. His motive is His name, which He has set among the nations through this people, and which they have made common.

That motive is not a cold one. The concern for His name is bound up with the knowledge that the nations should see who He is, 'Then the nations will know that I am the LORD', verse 23. It is a form of love for the world as well as for Israel, since a God whose name is profaned is a God whom the nations cannot know. Isaiah 48:9 to 11 has the same logic, 'For My own sake, My very own sake, I will act'. The glory of God and the good of His people are not rivals. They meet in a restored people who show God's holiness before the nations' eyes.

The chapter also shows that God works from the inside. He does not only change circumstances, bringing people back to a land and giving them rain. He changes the people, replacing a heart, giving a Spirit, making them able to keep what He commands. This is a doctrine of grace in its sharpest form: He commands what He gives. A God who asked for obedience but left the heart as it was would be asking for what He knew could not be produced. This God supplies what He requires.

He is holy and He is near. The image of the woman's impurity says that sin is real defilement before Him, and the Spirit placed within says that He dwells with those He has cleansed. Verse 28 puts it in the oldest terms, 'you will be My people, and I will be your God', and Revelation 21:3 gives the same words at the end of the story.

For worship, the passage teaches a few things. We pray 'hallowed be Your name' as a request that He would show His own holiness. We receive grace without boasting, since Ephesians 2:8 and 9 says it is a gift so that no one can boast. And we expect change, not merely forgiveness, trusting that the one who began a good work will carry it on to completion, Philippians 1:6. The shame of verse 31 is not wasted. It is the sign that He has been at work.

crossReferences.note: Jeremiah's announcement of the new covenant, in which God puts His law in their minds and inscribes it on their hearts, and forgives their iniquity. It is the closest parallel to Ezekiel 36:26 and 27 in content and the passage Hebrews 8 quotes in full. Taken together, the two prophets give the new covenant its inner change and its Spirit.

An earlier form of the same promise, spoken in the sixth year to the exiles: gathering from the countries, a new spirit, the stone heart removed and a heart of flesh given, so that they may follow His statutes. Reading 11:19 and 20 beside 36:26 and 27 shows how central the promise is to the book and how the idea grew.

The command that Ezekiel gives in the earlier chapter, 'fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit', and the appeal to repent and live. Set beside 36:26, where God gives the new heart, the two texts show that God commands what only He can give.

Moses foresees the exile and the return, and says that the LORD will circumcise their hearts so that they will love Him. It is the early root of Ezekiel's promise and shows that the problem of the heart was known from the start. The same sequence of scattering, gathering and inward change is found in both.

The rite of purification by water sprinkled on the unclean, which stands behind Ezekiel's promise of clean water in 36:25. It dealt with ritual defilement from death, and Ezekiel takes it up as a picture of God's cleansing of both impurities and idols.

God acts 'for My own sake, My very own sake', and will not yield His glory to another. It is the same logic as Ezekiel 36:22 and 32. It makes clear that the idea of acting for His name is a consistent feature of the prophets and not a surprising turn in Ezekiel.

The vision of the dry bones, which immediately follows. The Spirit enters the bones and they live, and the promise of verse 14 'I will put My Spirit in you and you will live' repeats 36:27. The two chapters work as a pair, one in the language of cleansing and heart, the other in the picture of resurrection.

Nicodemus comes to Jesus by night and is told that he must be born again, of water and the Spirit. Jesus's surprise that Israel's teacher does not understand shows that the teaching came from texts like Ezekiel 36. The wind and the Spirit of verse 8 also play on the ruach of Ezekiel.

Paul says the Corinthians are a letter written with the Spirit on tablets of human hearts, and that the new covenant is of the Spirit and not the letter. The contrast of stone and heart is Ezekiel's, and Paul shows that his own ministry is the fulfilment of the promise.

Salvation is not by righteous deeds but by mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ. It joins the water and the Spirit of Ezekiel 36:25 to 27 and gives them to the church. The theme of mercy without merit matches the denial in 36:22.

Peter explains Pentecost with Joel's prophecy that God will pour out His Spirit on all people. The promise of the Spirit that runs through Ezekiel 36 and 39 and Joel 2 is declared to be arriving. It shows that the first Christians saw the day as the beginning of the new covenant.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward the Bible tells of a people who cannot keep what God asks. Adam and Eve are given one command and break it. The generation of the exodus sees the sea parted and grumbles in the wilderness, and Moses is told even then that the LORD has not given them a mind to understand, Deuteronomy 29:4. The law is good, but it cannot change the heart, and the history of the judges and kings is the story of that failure. Ezekiel's chapter names the cause plainly: stone hearts. It is an honest diagnosis, and the book of Ezekiel has already pictured the heart as hardened in 2:4 and 3:7.

The chapter answers the problem by promising a different kind of covenant. The first covenant had instructions written on stone tablets, and this one places the Spirit inside the people. That is the thread that links Moses's hope in Deuteronomy 30:6, Jeremiah's new covenant, Joel's outpouring and Ezekiel's promise, and it is the promise whose fulfilment is the sending of the Spirit after Christ is raised, Acts 2:33. The story reaches its turning point at the cross, where Jesus says 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood', Luke 22:20.

The new covenant does not abolish the old purpose. It carries it out. The 'statutes' and 'ordinances' of verse 27 are still to be kept, and Paul says that Christ condemned sin in the flesh so that the righteous requirement of the law 'might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit', Romans 8:3-4. The fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22 and 23 is what a heart of flesh produces.

The land like Eden in verse 35 turns the story back to its beginning. The one who was driven from the garden is promised a garden again, and the story ends in Revelation 21 and 22, where the tree of life stands beside the river and God dwells with His people. The words of Ezekiel 36:28, 'you will be My people, and I will be your God', are repeated in Revelation 21:3 with the addition that 'God Himself will be with them'. Between those two verses lies the whole work of Christ and the Spirit, and every believer who has found a heart that loves what it once resisted is living inside the promise.

sermon.title: What Happens in the New Birth? Part 2
sermon.why: Though preached from John 3, Piper explicitly builds this message's central argument on Ezekiel 36:24-28, calling it 'the basis for the rest of this message,' tracing the sprinkled clean water and the new heart and new spirit given here as the Old Testament background to Jesus' words about being born of water and the Spirit, exactly the connection this study draws out.

quiz.q: Why does God say He will act to restore His people, verses 22 and 32?

options.text: Not for their sake, but to vindicate His own holy name, which they had profaned among the nations.
options.note: Both verses state this motive explicitly and repeat it for emphasis.

options.text: Because Israel had finally repented enough to earn restoration.
options.note: The text explicitly denies this: 'It is not for your sake that I will act.'

options.text: Because the surrounding nations demanded Israel's release.
options.note: No such demand from the nations is mentioned; God's motive is His own name, not external pressure.

options.text: Because Israel's suffering had simply run its natural course.
options.note: A specific theological reason is given, God's own name, not merely the passage of time.

quiz.q: What three things does God promise for His people's inner life in verses 25-27?

options.text: Sprinkle clean water on them, give them a new heart and new spirit, and put His own Spirit within them to cause them to walk in His statutes.
options.note: Verses 25-27 state each of these three promises in sequence.

options.text: Give them a new set of written laws to replace the old ones.
options.note: The promise concerns inward transformation and God's own indwelling Spirit, not a replacement legal code.

options.text: Grant them a new king who would enforce obedience by force.
options.note: No king or external enforcement is mentioned; the promise is internal transformation.

options.text: Nothing regarding their inner life; only their land is addressed in this section.
options.note: The inner life is the direct focus of verses 25-27, though land is addressed elsewhere in the passage.

quiz.q: What response does God say His restored people will have toward their own past, verse 31?

options.text: They will remember their evil ways and wicked deeds, and loathe themselves for their iniquities and abominations.
options.note: Verse 31 states this exact response, remembering and grieving over their sin even in restoration.

options.text: They will forget their past sins entirely and never think of them again.
options.note: The opposite is stated: they will remember, not forget.

options.text: They will blame their ancestors rather than take responsibility themselves.
options.note: The response described is personal self-loathing over their own deeds, not blame-shifting to ancestors.

options.text: They will feel no particular response toward their past at all.
options.note: A strong, specific emotional and moral response, self-loathing, is described directly in verse 31.

quiz.q: What will the nations conclude once God rebuilds and replants the land, verse 36?

options.text: That the LORD has rebuilt what was destroyed and replanted what was desolate, and that He has spoken and will do it.
options.note: Verse 36 states this conclusion directly, crediting the LORD with the restoration.

options.text: That Israel's own strength and wisdom restored the land.
options.note: The text credits the LORD explicitly, not Israel's own strength.

options.text: That the restoration was a natural, unremarkable event.
options.note: The restoration is presented as a deliberate divine act meant to be recognized as such by the nations.

options.text: The nations are not said to notice or conclude anything.
options.note: The nations' recognition of the LORD's work is the explicit point of verse 36.

quiz.q: What image does God use in verses 37-38 to describe how numerous His restored people will become?

options.text: As numerous as the flocks of sacrifices filling Jerusalem during her appointed feasts.
options.note: Verse 38 uses exactly this image of festival sacrificial flocks for the promised increase of people.

options.text: As numerous as the stars filling the night sky.
options.note: That image is used of Abraham's offspring in Genesis 15:5, not in this specific passage.

options.text: As numerous as the grains of sand on the seashore.
options.note: That image also belongs to the Abrahamic promise elsewhere, not this specific text.

options.text: No image of numerical increase is given in these verses.
options.note: A specific and vivid image, flocks at Jerusalem's feasts, is given directly in verse 38.

questions: God says He acts 'not for your sake... but for My holy name.' How does it change your view of God's grace toward you to know it flows from His own character rather than from anything you've earned?

The promise moves from external cleansing (clean water) to internal transformation (a new heart) to empowered obedience (God's own Spirit within). Which of these three truths do you most need to remember is already yours in Christ this week?

God's restored people don't forget their past sin; they remember it and are appropriately grieved by it, even while fully forgiven. How do you hold together genuine sorrow over past sin with the freedom of being fully cleansed?

The nations were meant to see God's restoration of Israel and know that He is the LORD. Where in your own life could God's work in you become a testimony others notice, not for your credit but for His name?

Jesus points Nicodemus, an expert in the Scriptures, back to this very passage and finds him unprepared to recognize it. Is there a familiar passage or promise of God's that you suspect you've read past without truly grasping what it offers you?

translationNotes.note: 'Sprinkle clean water' evokes the ceremonial washings of the Levitical law (compare Numbers 19:17-19) applied here to the whole nation's moral and spiritual defilement, not merely ritual impurity.

The Hebrew phrase for 'new heart' here (lev chadash) differs from the 'one heart' (lev echad) promised earlier in Ezekiel 11:19; the two passages use related but distinct wording to describe the same essential transformation.

'Let it be known to you' functions almost as a parenthetical aside, God pausing mid-promise to make sure His hearers do not mistake His mercy for their own merit before He continues describing the restoration.
